title: Ines and the Compass
premise: In 1917, Astrid Crane keeps a field hospital ledger on the Channel coast, quietly recording the names of wounded soldiers that officers strike from official reports. When a deserter named Ines arrives carrying a letter in the unmistakable handwriting of Captain Elias Vane — a man officially dead for six months — Astrid realizes the 'casualties' she has been logging were not casualties at all, but witnesses to a supply-line scandal the command means to bury. As military police close in and the tide turns, Astrid and Ines race to copy her ledger, smuggle it aboard a hospital ship, and get the truth on the record before the victors' historians can write their version. The book ends with the ship sailing at dawn: Ines gone with the pages, Astrid staying behind to face a tribunal, certain now that history happens to everyone — and that she has finally made herself part of the record.
about_author: Oscar Halloran is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters from the First World War. He writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She tends the wounded at a Channel-side field hospital and secretly records names the officers omit from dispatches. Establishes her belief that history happens elsewhere, to other people. Emotional beat: quiet, methodical defiance disguised as bookkeeping.

chapters.title: Struck Through
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. A dying private begs her to write his name down properly; his file arrives pre-marked 'deceased, no record.' Astrid begins to suspect the omissions follow a pattern tied to one supply convoy. Emotional beat: first crack in her detachment.

chapters.title: The Stranger at the Gate
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A mud-caked stranger slips past sentries at night, half-starved, clutching an oilskin packet. Matron wants him turned over; Astrid hides him in the linen store. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into instinctive loyalty.

chapters.title: Handwriting of a Dead Man
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Ines reveals the letter is signed by Captain Elias Vane, officially killed six months ago — the same name Astrid has seen struck through three times. Emotional beat: vertigo; two private obsessions suddenly colliding.

chapters.title: What Ines Carried
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. His story: he was Vane's batman, saw the convoy diverted and its witnesses listed as casualties, and ran when ordered to forget. The letter names names. Emotional beat: guilt of the survivor, relief of confession.

chapters.title: Matron's Warning
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Matron, no fool, warns Astrid that harboring a deserter will hang them both — then pointedly leaves a key to the records room. Emotional beat: unexpected solidarity between women who keep other people's secrets.

chapters.title: The Records Room
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Nighttime break-in to compare ledgers: eleven men reported dead who passed through her ward alive. She copies the first pages. Emotional beat: trespasser's thrill curdling into dread when she hears boots above.

chapters.title: Major Grell
chapters.summary: Grell's POV. The officer responsible for the 'corrections' arrives to inspect the hospital, courteous and cold, asking oddly specific questions about paperwork. He notices Astrid's careful hand. Emotional beat: menace wrapped in politeness.

chapters.title: Two Kinds of Duty
chapters.summary: Astrid and Ines, shared scene. Ines urges flight; Astrid refuses to abandon her patients or her ledger. Their argument becomes something closer to understanding — the first warmth between them. Emotional beat: love beginning as mutual recognition.

chapters.title: The Eleventh Name
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She finds the eleventh omitted man alive in a convalescent ward — a witness who can testify, if he'll speak. He is terrified, and Grell's aides have already visited him twice. Emotional beat: hope with a countdown attached.

chapters.title: Interrogation
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Grell interviews Astrid about 'irregularities in her ledger,' offering promotion for cooperation. She lies smoothly and hates how good she's become at it. Emotional beat: identity shifting — she is no longer a bystander.

chapters.title: The Witness Breaks
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The eleventh man agrees to sign a statement, then panics when Grell's men return; Ines gets him out through the coal cellar as the ward is searched. Emotional beat: terror, and the cost of courage measured in minutes.

chapters.title: Orders for the Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The hospital receives movement orders: patients and staff to be evacuated by a hospital ship sailing at dawn. Grell will control every document aboard. The deadline crystallizes. Emotional beat: trapped clarity.

chapters.title: Vane's Letter, Whole
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. He finally reads the full letter aloud: Vane is alive, hiding, and asks whoever holds the letter to finish what he started. Grief and fury mix — Ines thought himself a coward; Vane called him brave. Emotional beat: absolution he didn't ask for.

chapters.title: What We Owe the Dead Who Aren't
chapters.summary: Shared scene by lamplight. Astrid and Ines plan: copy the ledger, forge transport chits, hide the witness among genuine casualties, and board the ship themselves. They admit, almost accidentally, that they are afraid together. Emotional beat: love named without being spoken.

chapters.title: The Copying
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. A sleepless night duplicating the ledger in two hands, hiding one set in a Bible, one in her uniform lining. Matron covers for her one last time and takes the Bible 'for the chapel.' Emotional beat: handing your life to someone else's hands.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Gate
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. An orderly sells them out; Grell's military police take the witness and seal the docks. Ines escapes capture only because Astrid creates a diversion that gets her detained instead. Emotional beat: guilt inverted — the rescuer rescued.

chapters.title: The Tribunal Room
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Grell offers her a final bargain: surrender the ledger and Ines, or face charges of espionage. She recites the eleven names back to him, one by one, watching him flinch. Emotional beat: the climax of nerve — power reclaimed through memory.

chapters.title: Night Before the Tide
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. With Matron's help, Ines frees Astrid; they retrieve the hidden pages while sirens rise. The witness, released on a technicality Grell didn't foresee, joins them at the dock. Emotional beat: desperate, breathless momentum toward dawn.

chapters.title: Boarding
chapters.summary: Shared scene. On the gangplank, papers checked by a clerk who may or may not be sympathetic, the witness shaking, the ledger against Astrid's ribs. Grell arrives too late, held at the foot of the plank by protocol he worships. Emotional beat: triumph balanced on a knife edge.

chapters.title: The Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The ship pulls out; below deck, statements are signed and witnessed properly, on the record. Astrid chooses to disembark at the last port to face the tribunal and testify openly, sending Ines ahead with the duplicate pages. Emotional beat: sacrifice transformed into authorship of history.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Epilogue, dual POV. Months later: the inquiry opens, the eleven names read aloud in a courtroom; Ines watches from the gallery, Astrid testifies from the stand. Her ledger enters evidence, page one bearing her own name at last. Emotional beat: belonging — history happened to her, and she wrote it down.
